info.headline: Read short, illustrated texts to find the topic, key details, and main idea.
info.summary: Level A readers work with brief, high-support texts of one short paragraph, often paired with pictures, captions, or a simple chart. Tasks focus on locating explicit details, naming the main idea, and using picture and word clues to understand new vocabulary. Sentence frames, models, and word banks scaffold every item.
info.distinguishes: Texts are 1 short paragraph (about 3-5 simple sentences) with familiar, concrete topics and present-tense, single-clause sentences. Heavy support is built in: picture cues, word banks, sentence frames, and teacher models. Students answer literal 'right there' questions and order short sequences with explicit signal words; they are not yet expected to infer or compare across texts independently.

I can tell a fact from an opinion in a short sentence.

info.headline: Read informational passages to infer meaning, cite evidence, and analyze how texts are built.
info.summary: Level B readers work with longer, multi-sentence informational passages across science and social studies, including some compound and complex sentences. Tasks shift from literal recall to inference, selecting the strongest evidence, tracing cause and effect, and recognizing text structure and author's purpose. Support is lighter and students increasingly compare ideas across two texts and explain their thinking in writing.
info.distinguishes: Texts are longer (a full short paragraph to several sentences, sometimes two short passages) with abstract or academic topics and compound/complex sentences. Support is reduced to optional hints and frames rather than constant models. Students infer beyond the literal text, choose the best of several pieces of evidence, identify organizational structure, and write short evidence-based responses with growing independence.

info.headline: Read like an analyst: evidence, inference, vocabulary, and author's craft.
info.summary: Level C readers work with full informational and argumentative passages (200-350 words) in science, history, and math contexts, often paired with a table or chart. Tasks ask students to cite the sentence that best supports a claim, select all valid inferences, determine academic vocabulary from context, sequence historical events, compare two authors, and analyze why an author made a choice. Support is minimal and focused on test-taking reasoning.
info.distinguishes: Compared with Level B, Level C texts are longer and denser, with complex sentences, figurative and academic language, and integrated data. Questions require analysis rather than recall: evaluating which evidence is strongest, recognizing counterclaims, comparing authors' views, and explaining the purpose of a structure or detail. Distractors are closer to correct, so students must justify their choices.

activities.title: Author's Argument and Evidence
activities.directions: Read the editorial. Click the ONE sentence that states the author's main claim.
activities.prompt: Click the sentence that best states the author's main argument.
passage: Many middle schools have shortened recess to add more class minutes.
Students at our school should have a longer recess break each day.
Studies show that short outdoor breaks help students focus better when they return to class.
Teachers report fewer behavior problems on days when students get to move around.
Even a short walk can lower stress and improve memory.

activities.correct: Exactly! That sentence states what the author wants: a longer recess. The others are evidence.
activities.hint: A claim states an opinion or what should happen. Evidence gives facts and studies.
activities.support: A main claim often uses words like "should" and states a position, not just a fact.

activities.directions: Read the passage about rainforests. Choose ALL statements that the text supports.

passage: A tropical rainforest has several layers, each with different conditions.
The top layer, the canopy, blocks most sunlight from reaching the ground.
Because little light reaches the forest floor, few plants grow there.
Many animals live high in the canopy where food and sunlight are plentiful.
The forest floor is dark, damp, and covered with decaying leaves.

activities.correct: Strong synthesis! The text supports that the canopy gets more light, the floor has few plants, and the floor is damp and dark.

activities.title: Cite the Strongest Evidence: Street Trees
activities.skill: Selecting the evidence that best supports a claim
activities.directions: Read the argument and study the table. Then click the ONE sentence that gives the strongest evidence that trees make streets cooler.
activities.prompt: Which sentence gives the STRONGEST evidence that trees cool city streets?
passage: On a July afternoon last summer, students in Ms. Achebe's science class carried thermometers to two blocks near our school. On Carver Street, which is lined with tall oak trees, the sidewalk measured 88°F. Two blocks away on Fulton Avenue, where there are almost no trees, the sidewalk measured 119°F.

Our city should plant trees on every residential street that has fewer than five trees per block. The difference our class measured is not unusual. According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, shaded surfaces can be 20 to 45 degrees cooler than surfaces in direct sun. Cooler sidewalks mean cooler air, and cooler air means fewer families who must choose between paying for air conditioning and staying safe during heat waves.

Trees offer other benefits as well. Their leaves trap dust and pollution, and their roots soak up rainwater that would otherwise flood storm drains. Some neighbors say that trees drop messy leaves and that roots can crack sidewalks. These are real costs, but the city can choose smaller species with deep roots and organize volunteer leaf cleanups each fall.

A tree planted this year will shade a sidewalk for fifty years or more. That makes trees one of the least expensive ways to protect our neighborhoods from rising summer temperatures. The city council should fund a street tree program in next year's budget.

activities.title: Make Inferences: The Montgomery Bus Boycott
activities.skill: Selecting all valid inferences from a history text
activities.directions: Read the passage. Choose ALL the inferences the text supports. Be careful: some choices go beyond what the text says.
activities.prompt: Which inferences are supported by the passage?
passage: On December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks, a seamstress and an experienced civil rights activist, refused to give up her seat to a white passenger on a city bus in Montgomery, Alabama. Under the city's segregation laws, she was arrested. Her arrest became the spark for one of the most important protests of the civil rights movement.

Within days, Black leaders in Montgomery organized a boycott: they asked Black residents to stop riding city buses until the rules changed. This was a powerful choice, because Black riders made up about three-quarters of the bus company's passengers. A young minister named Martin Luther King Jr. was chosen to lead the new Montgomery Improvement Association.

Staying off the buses was not easy. Many people walked several miles to work each day in rain and cold. Others shared rides in a carpool system that used more than two hundred private cars, organized from churches across the city. Some participants lost their jobs, and leaders' homes were attacked, but the boycott continued.

The protest lasted 381 days. In November 1956, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that segregation on public buses was unconstitutional, and Montgomery's buses were integrated that December. The boycott showed that ordinary people, acting together and peacefully, could change unjust laws.

options.text: The boycott caused the bus company to lose a large amount of money.
Rosa Parks was the first person ever to refuse to give up a bus seat.
Churches played an important role in organizing the boycott.
Participants were willing to make real sacrifices for the protest.

activities.correct: Strong reading. Three-quarters of riders stopped paying fares (lost money), carpools were organized from churches, and people walked miles and lost jobs (sacrifice).
activities.hint: An inference must be backed by clues. Which choice claims a "first ever" that the passage never mentions?
activities.support: For each choice, find the sentence that supports it. If you cannot point to a clue, the inference is not supported.
activities.extension: Write one more inference about why leaders chose a boycott instead of another kind of protest. Cite a clue.
vocabulary: refusing to buy or use something as a protest

the unfair separation of people by race
segregación: separación injusta de las personas por su raza
not allowed by a country's constitution
inconstitucional: que no lo permite la constitución de un país

readFor: how people got around without buses

activities.title: Academic Vocabulary: Tiny Survivors
activities.skill: Using context to choose precise academic vocabulary
activities.directions: Read the passage about tardigrades. Choose the word that best completes each blank. Use the clues in each sentence.
activities.prompt: Complete the passage with the most precise academic words.
passage: Tardigrades, sometimes called water bears, are animals smaller than a grain of sand. They have eight stubby legs, each ending in tiny claws, and a round body that makes them look like miniature bears under a microscope. They were first described by a German scientist in 1773, and today scientists know of more than 1,300 species.

Tardigrades live almost everywhere on Earth, from the tops of the Himalayas to the bottom of the deep sea, and even in the damp moss growing on a city sidewalk. Most of them eat by piercing plant cells or tiny animals and sucking out the liquid inside. If you collect a clump of moss, soak it in water, and look at a few drops under a microscope, you have a good chance of finding one.

segments.text: What makes tardigrades famous is that they can
conditions that would kill almost any other animal. Scientists have tested them in

environments, from temperatures near absolute zero to more than 300°F, and even in the empty vacuum of outer space. When their home dries out, a tardigrade pulls in its legs, loses almost all of its water, and enters a
state called a tun, in which its body nearly stops working. It can stay this way for years. When water
, it swells back up and walks away within hours. Because they are so
, tardigrades help scientists study how living things might survive long trips through space.

activities.correct: Excellent. Withstand, extreme, dormant, returns, resilient: each word fits both the meaning and the clues around it.
activities.hint: Use context clues: "would kill almost any other animal" (so they survive it), "body nearly stops working" (inactive), "swells back up" (the water comes back).
activities.support: Read the whole sentence before choosing. Ask: does this word make sense with the clue words nearby?
activities.extension: Write your own sentence using resilient to describe a person or a plant.

activities.title: Word Meaning in Context: Day Zero
activities.skill: Determining the meaning of an academic word from context
activities.directions: Read the passage about Cape Town's water crisis. Then answer the vocabulary question.
activities.prompt: In paragraph 2, the word scarce most nearly means —
activities.passageTitle: The City That Almost Ran Dry
passage: In early 2018, the city of Cape Town, South Africa, faced a frightening possibility. After three years of very low rainfall, the reservoirs that supplied the city's four million people had dropped to about one-quarter of their capacity. City officials warned of "Day Zero," the day the taps in homes would be shut off and residents would have to collect a daily ration of water at public collection points.

Because water had become so scarce, the city limited each resident to 50 liters a day, about the amount used in a five-minute shower plus one toilet flush. Families collected the water from their showers in buckets and reused it to flush toilets. Farmers who relied on the same reservoirs agreed to reduce how much they took, and businesses installed equipment to recycle water.

The measures worked. By the time rain returned in mid-2018, Cape Town had cut its water use roughly in half, and Day Zero never arrived. Scientists who study water point to Cape Town as a warning and as a model. Climate change is making droughts longer in many regions, and cities that plan ahead, fix leaking pipes, and teach residents to conserve will be better prepared when water runs low.

options.text: dirty and unsafe to drink
available in very small amounts
very expensive to buy
frozen and hard to reach

activities.correct: Right. The reservoirs dropped to one-quarter, people were limited to 50 liters, and families reused shower water. All of these clues show there was very little water.
activities.hint: Look at what happened BECAUSE water was scarce: limits, rations, buckets. What would cause all of those?
activities.support: Context clues can come before and after a word. Here, the cause (low rainfall, low reservoirs) and the effects (limits) both point to the meaning.
activities.extension: Find another word in the passage that means almost the same as scarce or connects to it (hint: paragraph 3).

embalse: lago grande que guarda agua para una ciudad
a fixed amount someone is allowed to have
ración: cantidad fija que alguien puede recibir
to use carefully so it is not wasted
conservar: usar con cuidado para no desperdiciar
frames: Scarce means ___ because the text says ___.
A clue that helped me is ___.
readFor: what families did to save water

activities.title: Sequence History: The Journey of Paper
activities.skill: Ordering historical events from an informational text
activities.directions: Read the passage about how papermaking spread. Then put the events in the order they happened.
activities.prompt: Put the events in chronological order, from earliest to latest.
passage: Paper is so common today that it is easy to forget it once had to travel thousands of miles to reach most of the world.

Historians credit Cai Lun, an official in China's Han dynasty, with improving papermaking around the year 105 CE. He mixed tree bark, old rags, and hemp with water, pressed the mixture flat, and dried it into thin sheets. For centuries, China guarded the method closely.

The secret did not leave East Asia for more than six hundred years. According to traditional accounts, after the Battle of Talas in 751 CE, Chinese prisoners who knew how to make paper were brought to Samarkand, a trading city on the Silk Road. Soon, Samarkand became famous for its paper.

From there, the knowledge moved west with merchants and scholars. By about 800 CE, Baghdad had paper mills, and its scholars used paper to copy books on mathematics, medicine, and astronomy. Papermaking then spread across North Africa and reached Spain, where Europe's first paper mill operated by the 1100s.

Several centuries later, in the 1450s, Johannes Gutenberg's printing press in Germany depended on a steady supply of cheap paper. Without the long journey that began in China, the printing revolution might never have happened.

items.text: Baghdad has paper mills, and scholars copy books on paper.
Gutenberg's printing press depends on a supply of cheap paper.
Cai Lun improves papermaking in Han dynasty China.
Europe's first paper mill operates in Spain.
Papermakers are brought to Samarkand after the Battle of Talas.

activities.correct: Well done. China (105 CE), Samarkand (751), Baghdad (about 800), Spain (by the 1100s), Gutenberg (1450s).
activities.hint: Use the dates and time phrases: "around 105 CE," "in 751 CE," "by about 800 CE," "by the 1100s," "in the 1450s."
activities.support: Chronological order means time order. Make a quick timeline in the margin with each date from the passage.
activities.extension: Explain how the spread of paper connects to the Silk Road.
wida: Use dates and time signal words

activities.title: Author's Craft: Why Begin with Amara?
activities.skill: Analyzing the purpose of an author's structural choice
activities.directions: Read the article about ocean plastic. Then answer the question about the author's choices.
activities.prompt: Why does the author most likely begin and end the article with Amara's story?
passage: Amara Okoye was nine years old the first time she walked the beach near her grandmother's house in Lagos and counted bottle caps instead of seashells. She stopped at two hundred. "I thought the ocean was making them," she remembers. "I didn't understand that they came from us."

Amara's beach is not unusual. Scientists estimate that about 11 million metric tons of plastic enter the ocean every year, roughly a garbage truck's worth every minute. Unlike paper or food waste, most plastic does not break down. Instead, sunlight and waves crack it into smaller and smaller pieces called microplastics, which fish and seabirds mistake for food.

Much of this plastic is used only once. A water bottle may be used for ten minutes, but it can remain in the ocean for hundreds of years. Researchers say the most effective solutions start on land: reducing single-use packaging, improving trash collection in fast-growing cities, and designing products that are easier to recycle.

Today, Amara is fifteen and leads a youth cleanup group that has removed more than two tons of trash from Lagos beaches. But she says cleanups are not enough. "We can pick up plastic every Saturday," she says, "but if we keep making it this fast, the ocean will always win."

options.text: To prove that Lagos has the most plastic pollution in the world
To explain how microplastics are formed by sunlight and waves
To make a global problem feel personal and to frame the main message in a real person's words
To argue that beach cleanups are the best solution to ocean plastic

activities.correct: Exactly. Amara's story makes huge numbers feel human, and her final quote delivers the article's main idea: we must make less plastic, not just pick it up.
activities.hint: Notice that the middle paragraphs give the science and statistics. What does the story add that numbers alone cannot?
activities.support: Authors often open with an anecdote (a short true story) to hook readers, and close with a quote to drive home the main idea.
activities.extension: Explain how Amara's last quote connects to the solutions in paragraph 3.
wida: Explain the effect of an anecdote and quotation

activities.title: Text and Table: Budgeting the Class Trip
activities.skill: Integrating information from a text and a table to solve a problem
activities.directions: Read the passage and study the table. Use information from BOTH to answer the question.
activities.prompt: How much more money does the class need to raise at the car wash to pay for all student tickets and its share of the bus?
passage: Mr. Rahman's seventh-grade class wants to visit the science center in May. The class has 28 students, and the school requires one adult chaperone for every 7 students. Chaperones get in free, but each student ticket costs $12.

The bus company charges a flat fee of $180 for the round trip, no matter how many people ride. The class has already raised $280 from a bake sale, and the parent association has promised to pay for half of the bus.
The students recorded their costs and fundraising so far in a table so they could see how close they are to their goal. They plan to hold a car wash in April to raise the rest.

Before the car wash, the class must answer some questions. How many chaperones will they need? Which costs belong to the class, and which are paid by someone else? Once they subtract the money they already have, they will know exactly how many cars they need to wash. At $8 per car, every number matters, so the class treasurer, Lucía, plans to check each calculation twice before posting the goal on the classroom door.
activities.correct: Right. Tickets ($336) plus the class's half of the bus ($90) is $426. Subtract the $280 already raised: $426 – $280 = $146.
activities.hint: Add every cost the CLASS must pay, then subtract what it already raised. Remember: chaperones are free, and the parents pay half the bus.
activities.support: Multi-step problems: 1) list the costs, 2) add them, 3) subtract the money you have. Check each number against the passage.
activities.extension: If 2 more students join the trip, how many chaperones are needed, and how much more money must be raised? Explain.

activities.title: Find the Counterclaim: The Four-Day School Week
activities.skill: Identifying an author's counterclaim in an argument
activities.directions: Read the editorial. Click the ONE sentence where the author admits the other side has a reasonable point.
activities.prompt: Click the sentence in which the author acknowledges a counterclaim as reasonable.
passage: More than 900 school districts in the United States have switched to a four-day school week, usually by adding about an hour to each school day and closing on Fridays or Mondays. Supporters say the change saves money and gives families more time together. However, the evidence suggests that our district should keep the five-day week.

First, the savings are smaller than many people expect. A national study found that districts using four-day weeks saved only about 1 to 2 percent of their budgets, because teachers' salaries, the largest cost, stay the same.

Second, longer school days are hard on younger students. By the last hour of a longer day, many students are tired and learn less. Researchers in Oregon found that students in four-day districts scored lower in math and reading over several years than similar students in five-day districts.

Some families argue that a day off each week makes it easier to schedule appointments and gives students time to rest. This is a fair point. Yet for many working parents, the extra day off means finding and paying for childcare, and students who depend on school breakfast and lunch would lose those meals one day a week.
A small savings is not worth a loss in learning and a burden on families. Our district should keep its five-day week.

sentences.text: However, the evidence suggests that our district should keep the five-day week.
First, the savings are smaller than many people expect.
By the last hour of a longer day, many students are tired and learn less.

activities.correct: Yes. After describing what families argue, the author says "This is a fair point" to acknowledge the counterclaim, then answers it with "Yet."
activities.hint: A counterclaim is the other side's argument. Look for the sentence where the author agrees, for a moment, with people who disagree.
activities.support: Authors acknowledge counterclaims with phrases like "This is a fair point," "It is true that," or "Some argue," and then rebut with "Yet" or "However."
activities.extension: Identify the rebuttal that follows the sentence you chose. Is it convincing? Explain.

activities.skill: Comparing two authors' perspectives on one topic
activities.directions: Read the two short texts about homework. Then answer the question comparing the authors' views.
activities.prompt: Which statement best describes how the two authors' views differ?
passage: Text 1 — from a teacher's blog: Homework is practice, and practice is how skills become automatic. A musician does not learn a song only during lessons; she plays it at home until her fingers know it. In the same way, twenty minutes of math practice at night helps students remember what they learned in class. Homework also teaches responsibility, because students must manage their time without a teacher watching. When students skip practice, small gaps grow into big ones, and by the next unit they are lost. A short, focused assignment each night keeps those gaps from forming.

Text 2 — from a student newspaper: Homework is supposed to help students learn, but for many of us it mostly measures what is happening at home. Students who have a quiet room, a computer, and a parent who can help finish quickly. Students who care for younger siblings or share one phone for the whole family often cannot. A worksheet that takes one student fifteen minutes can take another student an hour, and the grade does not show the difference. If homework is given, it should be short, and students should be able to finish it during a study period at school, where everyone has the same quiet space, the same tools, and a teacher who can help.

options.text: Text 1 sees homework as useful practice that builds responsibility, while Text 2 worries that homework is unfair because home situations differ.
Text 1 wants homework banned, while Text 2 wants more homework.
Both authors believe homework should take at least an hour each night.
Text 1 focuses on music lessons, while Text 2 focuses on computers.

activities.correct: Right. The teacher compares homework to music practice and says it teaches responsibility; the student argues homework measures home resources, so it should be short or done at school.
activities.hint: Identify each author's main point first. Details like music or computers are examples, not the main view.
activities.support: To compare authors, ask: What does each one want? What reasons does each give? Where do they differ?
activities.extension: Write one sentence that both authors might agree with.

activities.title: Claim, Evidence, or Reasoning? School Gardens
activities.skill: Analyzing argument structure by sorting claim, evidence, and reasoning
activities.directions: Read the introduction, then sort each sentence from a student's argument about school gardens: is it the claim, evidence, or reasoning?
activities.prompt: Sort each sentence into Claim, Evidence, or Reasoning.
activities.passageTitle: Should Every Middle School Have a Garden?
passage: Two years ago, students at Riverside Middle School turned a weedy corner of the parking lot into a vegetable garden. Sixth graders built six raised beds out of donated lumber, seventh graders tested the soil in science class, and eighth graders designed a watering schedule so the plants survived the summer.

Today the garden grows tomatoes, peppers, collard greens, and herbs. Science classes use it to study plant life cycles and pollination, math classes measure plant growth and calculate harvest weights, and the cafeteria serves the vegetables in salads twice a month.
Many students and teachers now believe every middle school should have a garden like Riverside's. Below are sentences from an argument one eighth grader wrote for the school newspaper.

items.text: Every middle school should have a student vegetable garden.
At Riverside, science test scores on plant units rose 12 percent in the garden's first year.
This suggests that hands-on experience helps students understand and remember science concepts.
In a survey, 74 percent of Riverside students said they tried a new vegetable from the garden.
When students grow food themselves, they are more willing to try healthy foods, which can build lifelong habits.

activities.correct: Well done. The claim states the position, the evidence gives measured facts (12 percent, 74 percent), and the reasoning explains WHY the facts support the claim.
activities.hint: Evidence has numbers or facts. Reasoning explains what the facts mean, often with "This suggests" or "because." The claim uses should.
activities.support: Claim = what I think. Evidence = what proves it. Reasoning = how the evidence proves it.
activities.extension: Write one more piece of evidence and one more sentence of reasoning for this argument.
